newsitem.title: USA: Hillary will not get involved in Zaire problem.
newsitem.headline: Hillary will not get involved in Zaire problem.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton's six-nation tour of Africa includes a stop in Uganda but she will not use her visit to pressure Ugandan leaders to stop a rebel insurgency in Zaire, U.S. officials said on Thursday.
Ugandan-backed rebels fighting the Zairean government of autocratic French-backed President Mobutu Sese Seko have captured a swathe of eastern Zaire, driving Rwandan Hutu refugees before them.

President Bill Clinton's wife departs on Saturday on a two-week goodwill tour through Senegal, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Uganda and Eritrea. She will laud progress toward democracy and civil society, promote better rights for women and get in some safari sightseeing.

U.S. officials, briefing reporters on the first lady's trip on condition of anonymity, said Mrs. Clinton's March 27-28 visit to Uganda will emphasise the remarkable turnaround in Uganda in the years since the reign of now-exiled rulers Idi Amin and Milton Obote in the 1970s and 1980s.

A senior U.S. official said Washington already has made clear to Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni its concern about Uganda's role in the Zairean conflict and that the first lady would not use her courtesy calls on Ugandan officials for that purpose.

"There is no lack of opportunities to convey our concerns about the situation in Zaire. But this stop is focusing on Uganda as a model of economic reform, Uganda as a model for the progress of the transformation of women," the official said.

Mrs. Clinton will become the first lady to go on a solo goodwill tour of Africa. Her husband wants to make an African tour in the couple of years, which would make him the first president to go there during his term of office since Jimmy Carter two decades ago.
Her first stop is Dakar, Senegal. She will tour Goree Island, which was a hub for the slave trade, and visit Saam Njaay Village, where citizens are being trained in the institutions of democracy.
"I hope to witness first hand and to highlight each country's efforts to build democracy and a strong civil society," Mrs. Clinton said in a State Department speech on Wednesday.

In Cape Town, South Africa, Mrs. Clinton will attend a meeting of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, headed by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, which deals with apartheid-era crimes after Nelson Mandela was elected president in 1994.
The TRC, set up to heal apartheid's wounds, can grant indemnity from prosecution to those who confess to crimes or human rights abuses committed on either side of the race war.
Mrs. Clinton will also deliver a speech at the University of Cape Town and visit Robben Island, where many political prisoners were held during the apartheid years, including Mandela.

The first lady, accompanied by her 17-year-old daughter Chelsea, will get in plenty of sightseeing. She will tour Victoria Falls during her visit to Zimbabwe. In Tanzania she will see the Olduvai Gorge and the wildlife-covered plain of Serengeti.
